# Overconfidence and Recovery

Overconfidence is a common and often subtle risk in recovery from alcohol use disorder. It typically appears as thoughts like: *“I’ve got this under control now” “Just one wouldn’t be a big deal” “I’m not like I used to be”*

After a period of stability, it’s natural to feel stronger and more capable. Progress is real, but overconfidence can lead to underestimating risk.

Alcohol use disorder affects brain systems related to reward, memory, and decision-making. Even after time without drinking, these pathways can remain sensitive.

This means:

-   Old patterns can be reactivated quickly
-   The brain may recall the perceived benefits of drinking while minimizing past consequences
-   Risky situations may feel less risky than they actually are

## A Common Pattern

Overconfidence often follows a predictable shift:

“I need to be careful” → “I’m doing well” → “I’ll be fine” → increased risk

The danger is not confidence itself, but the loss of caution and structure that supports recovery. Which can lead to:

-   Entering high-risk environments without a plan
-   Letting go of protective habits (meetings, routines, supports)
-   Testing limits (*“just one,” “just this once”*)

![](https://github.com/jjcurtin/aud_support/blob/main/modules/images/overconfidence.png?raw=true){fig-align="center"}

::: {callout}
## A More Helpful Mindset

Recovery is strongest when confidence is balanced with awareness:

-   Confidence: *“I have tools and progress.”*
-   Awareness: *“I still need to protect my recovery.”*

A helpful reframe:

***“I’m doing well because I’m staying consistent, not because I no longer need the structure.”***

:::
